title: Landslides: what is standing fact
summary: A landslide is not the rain. The rain is the trigger; the slope is the disaster. Every hillside in the Himalaya and the Western Ghats holds loose material at an angle it can just about keep, and it keeps it until something changes — water in the pores, the toe cut away for a road, the trees that held the top thirty centimetres taken off, a quarry face a kilometre uphill. Then it goes in seconds, at night, on the people living below it, and it goes on going: the initial failure at Wayanad in 2024 became channelised debris flows that travelled eight kilometres. India has mapped where this can happen. What it has not done is count it.
summary_short: The rain is the trigger. The slope is the disaster — and what was done to the slope is a decision somebody made and can be read in the record.
india_relevance: About 0.42 million square kilometres of India, 12.6 per cent of the land area excluding snow-covered ground, is prone to landslide hazard: the two Himalayan arcs, the Western Ghats and Konkan hills, and a corner of the Eastern Ghats. That is where roads are being widened, hydropower built and hill towns extended, mostly on slopes whose susceptibility has been mapped at a scale that can tell you which valley is dangerous and not which slope above which village.

precedents.what: Mundakkai and Chooralmala, Wayanad, Kerala. 570 mm of rain in two days on slopes carrying tea farms; the failure became channelised debris flows that ran eight kilometres through the villages. Most of the dead worked on the farms, or were their families.

toll.label: — as of 6 August 2024; other credible counts run to 420, and there is no settled figure

precedents.what: Malin, Ambegaon taluka, Pune district, Maharashtra. A hillside came down on a sleeping village before dawn after days of rain. Deforestation, hill-cutting and the use of heavy excavators on the slope were all named at the time as contributing, alongside backwater from the Dimbha dam. Most of the dead died of asphyxia.

toll.label: — the count on 1 August 2014, two days in; the final official toll is widely reported as 151, which this pack has not traced to a primary return

precedents.what: The national register disagreed with a single event. NCRB's Table 1.0 filed 351 landslide deaths for the whole of India; the Wayanad landslide alone was confirmed at 392 with 150 missing. Neither figure is disputed by the body that published it. What separates them is the filing: NCRB counts deaths a reporting authority attributed to landslide, so deaths recorded under flood, or under the 1,626 with no named cause, or not returned in time, are simply not in the row.

toll.label: recorded landslide deaths, all of India, 2024 — against 392 at one site

precedents.card: The register is smaller than the event

mechanism.trigger: Water. Rain intense enough or prolonged enough to fill the pore space in the slope material, which removes the friction holding it together. There is no single national threshold: it depends on the material, the angle, the vegetation and how wet the slope already was, which is why forecasting a landslide is a different and much harder problem than forecasting the rain.
mechanism.conditions: Loose slope-forming material at a steep angle — weathered rock, old debris, laterite, tea and cardamom soils in the Ghats, glacial and fluvial deposits in the Himalaya. Susceptibility is a function of slope, geology, the material and the vegetation, and GSI maps it nationally at 1:50,000.
mechanism.assessment: The exposure is mapped and the annual count is not. GSI has a susceptibility map of 0.42 million km²; NRSC has ~80,000 mapped landslides over 25 years; NCRB has a deaths row that a single event can exceed. India knows where its slopes can fail far better than it knows how often they do, or how many people they kill.
mechanism.human: What was done to the slope, and what was built below it. Road and rail widening cuts the toe out from under a hillside; quarrying loosens it from above; terracing and levelling change where water goes; clearing the top of a slope removes the root mat that holds its first half-metre. None of these is weather. Down To Earth counted at least 48 stone quarries in Wayanad district from satellite imagery, 15 of them inside Ecologically Sensitive Areas and nine inside forests in ESA villages. The Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel reported in 2011; the High Level Working Group that replaced it reduced the protected extent; the environment ministry then accepted Kerala's request to cut its own ESA from 13,108 to 9,993.7 km². A decade on, not one of the states sharing the range has finalised its ESAs. That sequence is a record of decisions, not of rainfall.

causes.label: Rainfall-triggered slope failure
causes.short: Pore pressure rising in slope material until it loses friction.
causes.evidence: The rain gauge nearest the slope, and the antecedent fortnight. Usually available within a day; usually the first thing stated and the least contested.

causes.label: Channelised debris flow
causes.short: The failure entering a stream course and travelling far beyond the scar.
causes.evidence: The runout, on satellite imagery before and after. Distinguishing a flow from a slide decides where the danger was, and it is often settled only once a clear pass is available.

causes.label: The toe cut away
causes.short: Road, rail or building excavation removing support from the base of a slope.
causes.evidence: The cut face itself, and the date it was made. Visible on imagery and in project records, and rarely named in the first reporting.

causes.label: Quarrying above the failure
causes.short: Rock extraction loosening and loading the slope uphill of what fell.
causes.evidence: Quarry locations against the failure's catchment. Countable from imagery; contested in permits.

causes.label: What was taken off the slope, and what was put on it
causes.short: Clearing, plantation, terracing and construction changing how the slope holds water.
causes.evidence: Land-cover change over years, not days. This is the slowest cause to establish and the one most likely to be missing from an event page written in the first week.

what_to_watch.why: A slide, a debris flow and a slope collapse behave differently and are reported interchangeably in the first days.
A saturated slope stays dangerous after the failure, and most secondary landslides happen during the rescue.

what_to_watch.what: Whether the debris has dammed a river
what_to_watch.why: A valley-blocking landslide creates a lake that can breach later, moving the disaster downstream and days into the future.

what_to_watch.what: The toll and the missing, separately
what_to_watch.why: The two are combined and separated by different authorities on different days, which is most of the apparent disagreement between figures.

what_to_watch.what: What was on the slope before
what_to_watch.why: Cut faces, quarries and clearings are visible on imagery from before the event, and stop being visible after it.

what_later.why: Rehabilitation is often on ground that has not been assessed, because the assessment is at 1:50,000.
It can fail weeks after the landslide that made it, and it is nobody's event.

what_later.what: Whether the cause is investigated at all
what_later.why: Rain is announced within a day. Slope cutting and quarrying take an inquiry, and inquiries are not always published.

what_later.what: The next monsoon on the same slope
what_later.why: A failed slope is more likely to fail again, not less.
The same cutting and quarrying continues on slopes that have not yet failed, which is where the next one is.

not_counted: THE NATIONAL DEATH ROW IS SMALLER THAN ONE LANDSLIDE. NCRB's Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India 2024 records 351 landslide deaths for the whole country; the Wayanad landslide of 30 July that year was confirmed at 392 with 150 missing. A death reaches that row only if a reporting authority attributed it to landslide and filed it under that cause — so deaths filed under flood, deaths inside the 1,626 with no named cause at all, and deaths in returns that arrived late are outside it. The row is a floor and this site publishes it as one.

Landslides where nobody was looking. The pan-India seasonal inventory covers the 2014 and 2017 rainy seasons; the rest of the ~80,000 is event-based and route-wise, which means concentrated on the disasters somebody studied and the roads somebody surveyed. The record is thinner in the North East than the hazard is.

The slope above a village. National susceptibility mapping is at 1:50,000 — a scale that can say which valley carries the hazard and cannot say whether the hillside behind a particular row of houses will hold. GSI is upscaling to finer mapping on selected critical sectors; until that reaches a place, nobody living there has a map at the scale of their own risk.

Damage that is not death. Houses, livestock, cowsheds, terraces, roads and the season's crop are counted by state memoranda in rupees, on different definitions in different states, and are not aggregated nationally by cause.
withheld: 'Landslides in India are 66.5% North West Himalaya, 18.8% North East Himalaya, 14.7% Western Ghats' — widely repeated of the NRSC atlas, but the figures do not appear on ISRO's own page for the atlas and the landslide scientist who reviewed it reports no such split. It would in any case be a share of what was RECORDED, from an inventory whose pan-India layer is two rainy seasons.

'151 dead at Malin' — the final official toll is reported this way almost everywhere and is very probably right; it has not been traced to a primary return here, so the contemporaneous count of 56 confirmed and about 120 missing is what this pack states, with the 151 named beside it.

'Meppadi was one of 18 Ecologically Sensitive Localities named by the Gadgil panel in 2011' — repeated in several outlets after the 2024 landslide, and not traced to the panel report itself. The ESA facts this pack does carry are Down To Earth's, which are counted rather than recalled.

A death toll for the 2023 Himachal Pradesh monsoon. Credible figures run from about 320 to about 428 depending on who is counting and over what window, and the state's own Memorandum of Damages is the official series. Nothing here picks one, and no figure for that season is stated as this page's own.

An annual number of landslides in India. There is no national series that counts events per year: GSI maps susceptibility, NRSC maps a 25-year inventory, NCRB counts filed deaths. None of the three is an event rate, and adding them does not make one.

explainer.expands: Slope failure, and the debris flow it becomes
explainer.heading: What a landslide actually is
explainer.hook: The rain is the trigger. The slope is the disaster.
plain: Fill a bucket with damp sand and tip it out. It stands in a cone at a particular angle — steeper and it slumps. Every hillside is that cone, held at nearly the steepest angle it can manage.
Now pour water in. Water gets between the grains and takes away the friction that was holding them against each other. The angle that was just about fine is no longer fine.
That is why a landslide happens hours into heavy rain rather than at the first drop, and why a slope that has been wet for a fortnight fails in rain that a dry slope would have shrugged off.

And it is why what people do to a slope matters as much as the weather. Cut the bottom out for a road and the cone has nothing to sit on. Take the trees off the top and the first half-metre has nothing holding it. Blast rock above it and you have both loosened it and made it heavier. None of that shows up in a rainfall figure.
explainer.technical: The downslope movement of rock, debris or earth under gravity, triggered most often in India by rainfall raising pore-water pressure and reducing effective stress in the slope material. A failure that enters a stream channel becomes a debris flow and can travel kilometres beyond the source, as at Wayanad in 2024.
explainer.not: Not a flood, though it is often filed as one. Not an avalanche, which is snow and is a separate row in the national table. And not an act of weather alone: the trigger is rain, the cause is usually rain plus a decision.

india_watch: The Himalayan road and hydropower corridors — Rudraprayag and Tehri Garhwal above all, where landslide density and exposure of people and houses are both highest in the country — and the Western Ghats plantation belt from Wayanad through Idukki and Kodagu into the Konkan, where the slopes carry settlements, quarries and a monsoon that is arriving in shorter, harder bursts.
downstream: The stream course below the failure
The valley the dam would empty into
The road that was the only way in
_precedent_card: A SHORT CARD TITLE, AUTHORED — the place, or what the entry is about if it is not an event. The third entry here is about the register rather than a landslide, following flood.json, whose first precedent is CWC changing what it counts.
_figures_order: INDIAN FIGURES FIRST, then the event that contradicts them. `band` is scale | cause | india, as in glof.json; `supports` names an id from `causes`.
_withheld: FIVE FIGURES DELIBERATELY NOT PUBLISHED, each with the reason. Three of them are numbers that are probably true and were not traceable to a source this pack had read — which is the standard, not an apology for falling short of it.
